subject: Copywriting
title: The Unique Selling Proposition
description: A 1-minute de-risking session on The Unique Selling Proposition.

hook.text: Rosser Reeves argued every ad must make one clear proposition. One reason to buy. Only one.

buildup.text: His concept, the USP, meant finding what made a product different and hammering that point relentlessly.

discovery.text: 'M&Ms melt in your mouth, not in your hand.' Reeves wrote it. One claim, repeated for decades.

twist.text: Critics called it repetitive and boring. Reeves didn't care. Boring ads that sell beat clever ads that don't.

climax.text: The USP concept influenced every brand since. Find one thing, own it, repeat it until everyone knows.

punchline.text: One claim. Repeat forever. That's the USP.

quiz.question: What famous tagline did Rosser Reeves create?
options: M&Ms melt in your mouth, not in your hand

details.summary: Rosser Reeves formalized the Unique Selling Proposition in the 1940s: every ad must make a specific promise that competitors do not or cannot make. M&M's 'Melts in Your Mouth, Not in Your Hands' is the textbook USP. The concept forced brands to identify what made them genuinely different.
details.whyItMatters: The USP remains the foundation of brand strategy. In a crowded marketplace, the ability to articulate why your product is uniquely valuable is the difference between being chosen and being ignored.
takeaways: Each ad must propose a unique benefit the competition cannot offer
The M&M's slogan is the definitive USP example
USP thinking forces brands to find genuine differentiation

faq.question: How do you find a product's USP?
faq.answer: Examine what the product does that competitors do not. It could be a feature, ingredient, process, guarantee, or experience. The USP must be specific enough to be testable and meaningful enough to influence purchase decisions.

faq.question: Has the USP concept been replaced by branding?
faq.answer: Not replaced but evolved. Modern brand strategy combines USP-style differentiation with emotional positioning. The USP provides the rational foundation; brand personality provides the emotional wrapper. Both are needed for effective marketing.
